source_adaptation: Named information services, providers and qualification labels in the raw scheme are replaced by prepared generic route guides. Broad college and apprenticeship routes for baker and admin assistant were checked during preparation. The cards do not invent exact entry grades, course places or admission guarantees. Learners choose one career for the task without committing to it as a future job. Source progression and lateral moves remain included.
success: Map two distinct routes to one chosen career in order.
Identify qualifications, experience or skills needed for each using card clues.
Label entry, developed or still to check; add progression/lateral thinking separately.
prepare: Books, pens, prepared route cards A1/A2 and B1/B2, vocabulary mat and normal reading or typing aids. Keep the adult key apart from first responses. No web, login or pupil phone is needed.
activity: Retrieve work feature/question. Model a route and distinguish entry from learning. Compare college and apprenticeship pathways to baker. Choose baker or admin assistant, map both routes, identify requirements and possible progression/lateral moves. Feedback, fade and reflect.

evidence.description: Career-route comparison map: at least two distinct ordered routes to one chosen career, card labels and qualification, experience or skill requirements for each. Distinguish entry requirements, skills developed and details to check. Retain actual support and revision. Progression/lateral moves extend the map.

evidence_detail: Career-route comparison map: at least two distinct ordered routes to one chosen career, card labels and qualification, experience or skill requirements for each. Distinguish entry requirements, skills developed and details to check. Retain actual support and revision. Progression/lateral moves extend the map.
assessment: Week 5 is formative. Keep two distinct ordered routes to one chosen career, card labels, a qualification/experience/skill requirement for each and the entry/developed/check distinction. Keep first thinking, support and revision. Progression, a lateral move and an open question extend the map; record these separately from the exact core outcome. A list of two route names or two different careers is insufficient.
boundaries: Broad generic guides checked 30 October 2026. They are not applications, offers or a statement that a learner is eligible. Exact grades, equivalents, age rules, course level, support, places and funding need current individual checks before real action. No named providers, institutions, organisations, places or live addresses. Do not request grades, income or health disclosure. No practical food preparation, external application or account needed.
feedback: VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step. R requires Voice and Audience, NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult may be the audience. Use E only for actual banked evidence.
response_modes: Book first. Type instead is an optional equivalent record. Reader, scribe, speech, pointing and typing are normal access. A learner may explain the map privately. Their career choice is for this task and can change.

routes.Independent: Choose baker or admin assistant and use its two cards. Map two distinct routes in order to the same career. Identify a qualification, experience or skill each route requires and mark entry, developed or check. Add a possible later step or sideways move and a purposeful question. Use labels beside claims and explain one difference.
routes.Supported: Read one card and one field at a time. Offer two route headings and a shared career destination. Use a separate model, vocabulary and short prompts. Rehearse privately and retain at least two routes with a requirement for each as the target. Fade answer prompts where secure.
routes.Floor: Use A1/A2 and the short choices. Read aloud or scribe the learner’s own selections. Order both routes and add a requirement to each. Choices alone do not prove a complete map. Record missing elements or supplied answers as partial evidence.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Explicit instruction, a separate worked model and guided practice. Chunk by route and stage. Use the same entry, learning and next-step headings. Give extra processing time and return to the card clue.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Pre-teach route, qualification, apprenticeship and experience. Use private rehearsal and short frames. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. No cold calling or forced pair work.
adaptations.SEMH: Keep a predictable sequence, choice of career and private feedback. A task choice is not a final career commitment. No personal grades, family work or income disclosure required. Offer a regulation break and a clear return point.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Clear print, one-card view and normal aids. Allow pointing or spoken ordering before recording. Do not infer access to a route from a diagnosis or support need; identify support questions instead.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Explain route as a sequence of steps. Model entry versus learning with simple examples. Rehearse privately, then record the learner’s reasoning with normal language support.

hinge: A1 and A2 both aim at baker. Which statement fits? A: A1 guarantees a job when the course ends. B: A1 needs a later job application; A2 combines work and training. Answer B. Ask for both card clues. If insecure, separate study, application and work, re-model, then use the parallel hinge.
parallel_hinge: B2 says office skills develop during training. Which statement fits? A: Every skill listed must be mastered before entry. B: Check entry needs separately from skills learned on the route. Answer B. Ask for the entry and learning lines. If insecure, retain supported mapping and log the missing distinction.
frames: F: “My career is ... . First ... . Then ... .” M: “Route ... needs ... . The card says ... . This is for entry / learned / to check.” H: “Both routes can lead to ... , but ... . A later move could be ... if ... .”
misconceptions: “There is one route to each career.” The paired cards show distinct routes to the same destination. “A course or level guarantees a job.” Entry, completion and employment are separate decisions. “All skills are entry requirements.” Some develop during training. “A higher level means a better person or the best route.” Level concerns learning demand, not worth or automatic fit.
ta_focus: I do: check sequence and the difference between entry and learning. We do: prompt a card clue, not a preferred answer. Independent: keep the learner’s chosen career, log actual support and fade prompts. Rehearse one question for a later careers conversation.
prompt_ladder: 1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.

steps: Build skills at work as a baker
route_cards.entry: Course entry rules vary. Check which school qualifications, including English and maths, are asked for. No fixed grades are given here.
route_cards.learning: Learn to measure, follow a recipe and work safely with food. Complete the course tasks and checks for its qualification. Check the course level.
route_cards.experience: Practical course tasks build experience. A work placement may help, if offered. The course does not promise a job.
route_cards.progression: With experience and further training, a baker could move into a team lead role. A move into bakery sales uses some related skills.
route_cards.check: What are the course entry rules, level and work practice options?

steps: Learn at work and in training
Complete the training and skills checks
route_cards.entry: Apply for an available place. The employer sets entry needs. English and maths qualifications, or equivalents, may be asked for. Check the exact rules.
route_cards.learning: A Level 2 baker apprenticeship is one route. Develop baking, measuring, food safety and team skills. Show these skills in the required checks.
route_cards.experience: Work is part of this route, alongside training. You learn in the job. Prior paid bakery work is not stated as a fixed rule in this guide.
route_cards.progression: After training, seek a baker role or more training. A later team lead role needs further skill and experience. Continued work is not promised.
route_cards.check: What entry skills are needed, and how are work and training arranged?

steps: Build skills through work and training
route_cards.entry: Course entry rules vary. Check the school qualifications and English or maths needed. This guide does not give fixed grades.
route_cards.learning: Build skills in writing clear messages, keeping records and using office software. Complete course work and checks. Check its qualification and level.
route_cards.experience: Course tasks can show office skills. An agreed office placement or volunteer role may add experience. It is not a fixed entry rule here.
route_cards.progression: With experience, an admin assistant could seek a team lead role. A move to another office team may need extra training.
route_cards.check: What are the entry rules, course level and chances to practise office tasks?

steps: Learn at work and in training
Complete the training and skills checks
route_cards.entry: Apply for an available place. Entry needs depend on the employer and level. Check school qualifications, English, maths and any skills test.
route_cards.learning: A Level 3 business administration apprenticeship is one route. Develop clear communication, accurate records, office software and planning skills. Complete the required checks.
route_cards.experience: Work tasks and training build office experience. Show what you can do as you learn. This guide does not set a fixed amount of prior paid work.
route_cards.progression: After training, seek an admin role or further training. With experience, a team lead role or a move to another office team may be possible.
route_cards.check: What entry needs apply to this level, and what support is available?

route_status: Prepared route guides, checked 30 October 2026. These are broad routes, not offers of a course or job. Exact entry rules and places must be checked.
comparison_fields: Ordered steps to the same career
Entry need or detail to check
requirement_evidence_rule: Identify a qualification, experience or skill for each route. Label entry, developed or still to check. An unanswered entry question alone does not replace a known skill requirement. Same chosen career at both destinations.

route_verification.scope: College and apprenticeship routes to baker and admin assistant; Level 2 baker and Level 3 business administration examples; generic work skills and possible progression.
route_verification.method: Public occupational guidance and current apprenticeship information inspected during preparation. Private source check retained; names, live addresses and raw pages excluded from the delivered pack.
route_verification.limits: Broad route legitimacy only. No actual place, individual eligibility, fixed entry grades, funding, offer or guaranteed employment verified. Exact details require a current check before real action.

paragraphs_in_document_order: Teacher and cover planner
Routes, qualifications and progression
Tuesday 1 December 2026 · P3 · 40 minutes · Year A
GROW · up to five learners · Independent is the default
Unit: Identity & Belonging — Belonging in work
Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
Exact source outcome
I can map at least two routes into a chosen career and identify qualifications, experience or skills each requires.
Weekly outcome: Students research entry routes and understand that several routes may lead to the same occupation.

Source: specialist Careers scheme, GROW Careers physical row 13, Autumn 2 row 5. E13 weekly outcome; F13 focus; G13 exact outcome; H13 sequence; I13 timing; J13 evidence; K13 access; L13 support; M13 end check; N13 formative.
Question and success checks
How could two routes lead to the same career?

1. Map two distinct routes to one chosen career in order. 2. Identify qualifications, experience or skills needed for each, using card clues. 3. Label what is needed at entry, learned during training or still to check. A later move is an added progression check.
Prepare
Books, pens, prepared route cards A1/A2 and B1/B2, vocabulary mat and normal reading or typing aids. Keep the adult key apart from first responses. No web, login or pupil phone is needed.
Source adaptation

Named information services, providers and qualification labels in the raw scheme are replaced by prepared generic route guides. Broad college and apprenticeship routes for baker and admin assistant were checked during preparation. The cards do not invent exact entry grades, course places or admission guarantees. Learners choose one career for the task without committing to it as a future job. Source progression and lateral moves remain included.
Where this leads
This helps me see more than one next step towards work and ask what I need to learn or check.
Forty minute teaching sequence
Phase
Min
Teaching and evidence
Retrieval
Recall a work feature and a question from Week 4. Fallback: people can reach the same job in different ways.
Explicit input
Explain route, qualification, experience and skill. Model A1 in order. Separate entry needs from skills learned. Check the card label, date and limits.
Guided analysis
Compare A1 and A2 to the same baker destination. Use the main hinge, re-model if needed and use the parallel hinge. Identify one later step and a sideways move.
Independent application
Choose baker or admin assistant. Map both matching cards to that career. Add requirements to each branch, label entry/developed/check and keep one question. Feedback and prompt fade.
Reflection
Explain two routes and a key requirement for each. Check source clues and sequence. Retain map, support and revision in the Careers Portfolio/action plan.
5 + 7 + 10 + 13 + 5 = 40 minutes. Checks, feedback, processing and access pauses sit within these phases. Slide 11 is an access reference; slide 12 is hidden for staff.
Worked example and fade

Model A1: School; a bakery or catering course; apply for trainee bakery work; build skills as a baker. Measuring and food safety develop during study and work. Course entry qualifications and level need checking. Course completion does not guarantee a job. Point to the A1 label and its entry, learning and experience lines.

Fade: keep the headings, then let learners build A2 and find its requirements. Remove the completed model before independent mapping where secure. Retain normal reader/scribe access. A copied branch alone is not evidence of independent understanding.
Check after explicit input

Is a skill learned during the course always needed before entry? Expected no. Does a course offer guarantee a job? Expected no. Ask the learner to show which card line supports each answer. Re-model entry, learning and the later job application if unclear.
Routes and planned access
Independent

Choose baker or admin assistant and use its two cards. Map two distinct routes in order to the same career. Identify a qualification, experience or skill each route requires and mark entry, developed or check. Add a possible later step or sideways move and a purposeful question. Use labels beside claims and explain one difference.
Supported

Read one card and one field at a time. Offer two route headings and a shared career destination. Use a separate model, vocabulary and short prompts. Rehearse privately and retain at least two routes with a requirement for each as the target. Fade answer prompts where secure.
Floor

Use A1/A2 and the short choices. Read aloud or scribe the learner’s own selections. Order both routes and add a requirement to each. Choices alone do not prove a complete map. Record missing elements or supplied answers as partial evidence.
Cognition and Learning

Explicit instruction, a separate worked model and guided practice. Chunk by route and stage. Use the same entry, learning and next-step headings. Give extra processing time and return to the card clue.
Communication and Interaction
Pre-teach route, qualification, apprenticeship and experience. Use private rehearsal and short frames. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. No cold calling or forced pair work.
SEMH

Keep a predictable sequence, choice of career and private feedback. A task choice is not a final career commitment. No personal grades, family work or income disclosure required. Offer a regulation break and a clear return point.
Sensory and Physical
Clear print, one-card view and normal aids. Allow pointing or spoken ordering before recording. Do not infer access to a route from a diagnosis or support need; identify support questions instead.
EAL
Plan in any language. Explain route as a sequence of steps. Model entry versus learning with simple examples. Rehearse privately, then record the learner’s reasoning with normal language support.
Record usual access separately from prompts that supply an answer. Keep normal aids while answer scaffolds fade. Use the source routes Independent / Supported / Floor.
Staff prompts and checks
Hinge during guided comparison

A1 and A2 both aim at baker. Which statement fits? A: A1 guarantees a job when the course ends. B: A1 needs a later job application; A2 combines work and training. Answer B. Ask for both card clues. If insecure, separate study, application and work, re-model, then use the parallel hinge.
Parallel hinge

B2 says office skills develop during training. Which statement fits? A: Every skill listed must be mastered before entry. B: Check entry needs separately from skills learned on the route. Answer B. Ask for the entry and learning lines. If insecure, retain supported mapping and log the missing distinction.
Speaking frames

F: “My career is ... . First ... . Then ... .” M: “Route ... needs ... . The card says ... . This is for entry / learned / to check.” H: “Both routes can lead to ... , but ... . A later move could be ... if ... .”
TA focus

I do: check sequence and the difference between entry and learning. We do: prompt a card clue, not a preferred answer. Independent: keep the learner’s chosen career, log actual support and fade prompts. Rehearse one question for a later careers conversation.
Prompt ladder
1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.
Misconceptions and corrections

“There is one route to each career.” The paired cards show distinct routes to the same destination. “A course or level guarantees a job.” Entry, completion and employment are separate decisions. “All skills are entry requirements.” Some develop during training. “A higher level means a better person or the best route.” Level concerns learning demand, not worth or automatic fit.
Evidence and source end check

J13: Career-route comparison map. M13: Can the student identify two legitimate routes and their key requirements? Keep two ordered routes to the same career and route-specific qualification, experience or skill evidence. Mark exact entry details as unknown where the cards do not give them. Add progression/lateral thinking without treating it as a third compulsory route.
Evidence feedback and boundaries
What this lesson can evidence

Week 5 is formative. Keep two distinct ordered routes to one chosen career, card labels, a qualification/experience/skill requirement for each and the entry/developed/check distinction. Keep first thinking, support and revision. Progression, a lateral move and an open question extend the map; record these separately from the exact core outcome. A list of two route names or two different careers is insufficient.
Response and feedback

Book first. Type instead is an optional equivalent record. Reader, scribe, speech, pointing and typing are normal access. A learner may explain the map privately. Their career choice is for this task and can change.

VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step. R requires Voice and Audience, NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult may be the audience. Use E only for actual banked evidence.
Portfolio

Retain the route map, source clues, requirement labels, support and revision in the Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. Staff confirm any accredited mapping from actual work; no completion inferred. Use the open question as a next research step.
Teaching need next lesson ____________________ Next research question ____________________
Boundaries

Broad generic guides checked 30 October 2026. They are not applications, offers or a statement that a learner is eligible. Exact grades, equivalents, age rules, course level, support, places and funding need current individual checks before real action. No named providers, institutions, organisations, places or live addresses. Do not request grades, income or health disclosure. No practical food preparation, external application or account needed.
Calendar and sequence

Year A. Autumn 2 Week 5, 30 November–4 December 2026. Tuesday 1 December, P3, 40 minutes. Week 6 retains mixed formative/summative source marking; Week 7 is assessing. Weeks 6–7 follow in order, one return after each Downloaded.

Requirements and sequence

Keep two routes to the same chosen career. Put steps in order and identify a qualification, experience or skill needed for each. Label entry, developed or check. A course does not guarantee a job; a training skill is not automatically an entry requirement.

Staff answers and route guide
Scope and outcome
Prepared route guides, checked 30 October 2026. These are broad routes, not offers of a course or job. Exact entry rules and places must be checked.
Exact outcome: I can map at least two routes into a chosen career and identify qualifications, experience or skills each requires.

The cards summarise credible broad routes, not fictional admissions criteria. Exact entry grades, equivalent qualifications, age rules and current places are deliberately not specified. Requirements can include skills to develop and demonstrate during training; label them distinctly from entry requirements.
Baker routes
Field
A1 college
A2 apprenticeship
Sequence
School; bakery/catering course; apply for trainee work; develop at work.
School; apply for a place; work plus training; complete training and checks.
Entry
Check course qualifications, English/maths and level.
Employer and programme entry needs vary; check exact requirements.
Learning and qualification
Measuring, recipes and food safety; assessed course qualification, level to check.
Level 2 baker route; baking, measurement, food safety and team skills, with checks.
Experience
Course practice; a placement may help if offered.
Work experience is built into work and training.
Next move
Possible team lead role with experience; possible bakery sales move.
Seek baker work or further training; later leadership needs more skill and experience.

Core difference: A1 includes a job application after course study; A2 combines a job with training. Neither promises a future permanent role. Do not change “may be asked for” to a universal entry requirement.
Admin routes and wider choices
Field
B1 college
B2 apprenticeship
Sequence
School; business/admin course; apply for admin work; develop through work/training.
School; apply for admin apprenticeship; work plus training; complete training/checks.
Entry
Check course entry qualifications, English/maths and level.
Check employer needs and level, qualifications and any skills test.
Learning and qualification
Clear messages, records and office software; assessed course award, level to check.
Level 3 business administration is one route; communication, records, software and planning.
Experience
Course tasks; agreed placement or volunteering may help.
Office experience grows through work tasks and training.
Next move
Possible team lead role or another office team with further learning.
Possible admin role, more training or later team/role move.
Progression and lateral moves

Progression: more advanced training or a team lead role after further development. Lateral move: bakery sales or a different office team using related skills. These require checking and may need more training. Do not present promotion or a job as automatic.
Wider route context

School may lead to further study at a college or sixth form, work with training or an apprenticeship. Some routes can later lead to higher education. The selected baker/admin routes do not require a degree by default. Do not make a universal level-to-level ladder or imply that all qualifications at a level cover the same subject.
Checks and misconceptions
Retrieval and model

Recall a feature and question from Week 4, without assuming prior completion. Fallback: the same career can have different routes. After A1 model, expected answers: skills can develop during training; a course does not guarantee a job. Ask for the card lines.
Main hinge
B is correct. A1 includes later application for bakery work; A2 combines work and training. Re-model stage and application if needed. Then use the parallel hinge.
Parallel hinge
B is correct. Entry needs and skills developed during B2 are separate. Ask for one example of each or an entry detail to check. Keep supported work if the distinction remains insecure.
Misconceptions

One career can have several routes. Route type and qualification level are different ideas. Level is not a ranking of people or a guarantee of suitability. Courses, apprenticeships and jobs have distinct entry and completion decisions. “Useful experience” is not automatically a compulsory entry condition. Unknown grades must stay unknown.
Supported and Floor

Floor key A, A, B, A, B, A. Ask for two ordered branches and a requirement for each beyond the choices. Learners can choose a career simply for this task. No personal grades or fixed ambition is needed. Record supplied answers separately from reading/scribing.
Safe discussion

Use unnamed generic types and prepared cards. No real application or contact is made. Do not steer learners away from a route because of diagnosis or support needs. Rehearse questions about access and support privately, without health or family disclosure.
Evidence and feedback guide
Core evidence

J13 calls for a career-route comparison map. G13 requires at least two routes to one chosen career and qualifications, experience or skills each requires. M13 checks two legitimate routes and key requirements. Keep card labels, ordered steps and at least one accurate requirement per route, showing whether it is at entry, developed or still to check. A question alone does not replace a known skill requirement.
Secure and partial evidence

Secure example: “I chose baker. A1: school, bakery course, apply for trainee work, develop as a baker. I learn measurement and food safety; entry grades need checking. A2: apply for an apprenticeship, work plus training, complete checks. It develops baking and team skills at Level 2.” A later team lead role requires more skill and experience.

Partial: two labels without steps; routes to different careers; only one route; no requirement for one branch; a copied model; or made-up entry grades. Added progression and lateral moves extend the map, but do not replace the two core routes.
Precise next steps

“Keep the same career at the end of both routes.” “Put the steps in order.” “Add a skill needed on the second route.” “Separate entry needs from what you learn.” Set one next step and keep the response.
Access and independence

Normal reader, scribe, typing or aids do not by themselves reduce independence of thought. Log actual answer prompts, then fade where secure. Accept a private explanation or ordered pointing with a scribed record.
Portfolio and marking

Retain map, labels, requirements, actual support and revision in the Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. VF verbal feedback; WS supported; I independent; NS next step in green; // self-edit; ? read back; E actual banked evidence; R after Voice, Audience, NS and response in in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode.
Fidelity boundary

Exact G13 outcome, I13 sequence and K13 routes retained. Prepared generic cards replace named/live sources in H13 at the owner’s direction. Progression and lateral moves retained. Week 5 formative; Week 6 mixed source marking; Week 7 assessing.
Two routes to baker
Prepared route guides, checked 30 October 2026. These are broad routes, not offers of a course or job. Exact entry rules and places must be checked.
A1 College course
Steps: 1. School; 2. Bakery or catering course; 3. Apply for trainee bakery work; 4. Build skills at work as a baker.
Entry: Course entry rules vary. Check which school qualifications, including English and maths, are asked for. No fixed grades are given here.
Learning: Learn to measure, follow a recipe and work safely with food. Complete the course tasks and checks for its qualification. Check the course level.
Experience: Practical course tasks build experience. A work placement may help, if offered. The course does not promise a job.
Later: With experience and further training, a baker could move into a team lead role. A move into bakery sales uses some related skills.
Check: What are the course entry rules, level and work practice options?
A2 Apprenticeship
Steps: 1. School; 2. Apply for a baker apprenticeship; 3. Learn at work and in training; 4. Complete the training and skills checks.
Entry: Apply for an available place. The employer sets entry needs. English and maths qualifications, or equivalents, may be asked for. Check the exact rules.
Learning: A Level 2 baker apprenticeship is one route. Develop baking, measuring, food safety and team skills. Show these skills in the required checks.
Experience: Work is part of this route, alongside training. You learn in the job. Prior paid bakery work is not stated as a fixed rule in this guide.
Later: After training, seek a baker role or more training. A later team lead role needs further skill and experience. Continued work is not promised.
Check: What entry skills are needed, and how are work and training arranged?
Two routes to admin assistant
Prepared route guides, checked 30 October 2026. These are broad routes, not offers of a course or job. Exact entry rules and places must be checked.
B1 College course
Steps: 1. School; 2. Business and admin course; 3. Apply for an admin job; 4. Build skills through work and training.
Entry: Course entry rules vary. Check the school qualifications and English or maths needed. This guide does not give fixed grades.
Learning: Build skills in writing clear messages, keeping records and using office software. Complete course work and checks. Check its qualification and level.
Experience: Course tasks can show office skills. An agreed office placement or volunteer role may add experience. It is not a fixed entry rule here.
Later: With experience, an admin assistant could seek a team lead role. A move to another office team may need extra training.
Check: What are the entry rules, course level and chances to practise office tasks?
B2 Apprenticeship
Steps: 1. School; 2. Apply for an admin apprenticeship; 3. Learn at work and in training; 4. Complete the training and skills checks.
Entry: Apply for an available place. Entry needs depend on the employer and level. Check school qualifications, English, maths and any skills test.
Learning: A Level 3 business administration apprenticeship is one route. Develop clear communication, accurate records, office software and planning skills. Complete the required checks.
Experience: Work tasks and training build office experience. Show what you can do as you learn. This guide does not set a fixed amount of prior paid work.
Later: After training, seek an admin role or further training. With experience, a team lead role or a move to another office team may be possible.
Check: What entry needs apply to this level, and what support is available?
A model and your route map
A1 model for baker
First: school. Next: a bakery or catering course. Then: apply for trainee bakery work. Build skills at work as a baker.
On this route I learn to measure and work safely with food. I must check the course entry rules and level. A course place does not promise a job.
Your task in your book
Choose baker with A1/A2, or admin assistant with B1/B2. Keep the same career at the end of both routes.

For each route, show steps in order. Add a qualification, experience or skill it needs. Mark each point: needed at entry, learned on the route, or still to check. Keep the card label beside your point.
Add one possible later step and one sideways move. These may need more training. Keep a useful question. Your task choice is not a final job choice.
Other routes and moves

After school, a college course, a sixth form, work with training or an apprenticeship may be options. Further study, including higher education, can follow some routes. Check the needs of the chosen job and course. A degree is not required for every career.
Progression can mean more skill or responsibility. A sideways move uses skills in a related role. For example, a baker might move into bakery sales after more learning.
Read, point, speak, write, type or use a scribe. Plan in any language. Keep your first view and any change.
Floor choices and short frames
Use A1 and A2 with the cards in view. An adult may read and record your own choices.

My two routes
“My career is ... . Route one is ... . First ... . Next ... . Route two is ... . First ... . Next ... .”
“For route ... , I need to learn ... . At entry, I would check ... .”
Order both routes and show a need for each. A choice on its own is not a full map. You may explain your map in private.

Keep normal access separate from answers supplied. Record a missing route, skill or sequence as partial. A later move is possible, not promised. The same job choice can have more than one sensible route.
Words for career routes
Word
Meaning
route
A series of steps towards a goal.
qualification
A formal award for learning that has been checked.
level
The demand of the learning. Check the exact award.
college course
Study and practice in a subject or job area.
sixth form
A place to study after the main years of secondary school.
apprenticeship
A job that includes planned training.
entry requirement
Something needed to start a course or role.
experience
Knowledge and practice gained by doing things.
skill
Something you can do and develop through practice.
progression
Moving on in learning, skill or responsibility.
sideways move
A move to a related role, rather than a higher role.
higher education
Study beyond school or college, such as a degree.

Distinguish entry requirements, skills developed and details to check. Retain actual support and revision. Progression/lateral moves extend the map.
